name: Handshake
tech: A handshake is the exchange that two systems use to establish a working connection. Once it completes, the actual work can begin.
examples: Starting a new job
Making a relationship official
Signing a contract
Joining a team or partnership
Initiating a creative collaboration
reflection: A handshake establishes a working connection. Two systems exchange information, confirm that they can work together, and then begin communicating. In computing, the uncertainty ends there. In life, starting something new can still feel uncertain even when the decision to do so feels right. With time, things will often begin to feel more natural.

name: Bridge
tech: A network bridge connects two network segments so traffic flows between them. More broadly, a bridge links two systems built on different terms.
examples: Trying to help two people understand each other
Helping a partner understand your family or vice versa
Explaining a job to people outside the field
Mediating a conflict
Moving between different cultural or social environments
reflection: A bridge allows communication between separate systems. Because each side operates differently, information often has to be translated as it moves across. In life, people sometimes play a similar role between different groups or perspectives. Spending time in more than one world can broaden the sense of what feels possible or understandable.

name: Loopback
tech: Loopback is when a system communicates with itself, often useful for testing.
examples: Rehearsing a conversation in your head
Revising an unsent message
Ruminating on something that happened
Imagining what someone would say
Wavering on a decision
reflection: A loopback routes a signal back into the same system that produced it. No outside input enters the exchange. In computing, loopbacks are useful for testing, calibration, and internal communication. In life, people often do something similar when rehearsing difficult conversations, struggling to make decisions, or trying to predict outcomes. Internal reflection can clarify things up to a point, but some questions only become clearer through input from the outside world.

name: Echo
tech: An echo is the return of a signal in the same form it was sent.
examples: Repeating the same conflict in different relationships
Falling into the same role in every social group
Recreating dynamics learned earlier in life
Returning to familiar habits under stress
Having the same argument over and over
reflection: An echo is a signal that returns in the same form it was sent. In computing, echoes can confirm that a connection exists, but they do not provide new information. In life, repeated patterns can start to feel inevitable simply because they are so familiar. The same expectations and reactions repeat until they begin reinforcing themselves. Sometimes change only becomes possible when outside input interrupts the pattern.

name: Static
brief: Too much noise obscures what matters.
tech: Static is random noise that gets mixed into a transmission and makes the actual signal hard to hear.
examples: Struggling to focus amid constant interruptions
Sorting through conflicting advice
Confusing urgency with importance
Trying to choose what you want from too many options
Trying to think clearly while overwhelmed
reflection: Static is noise that interferes with a signal without replacing it entirely. The message is still there, but it becomes harder to separate from everything competing with it. Human situations can feel similar. In life, clarity can become harder to maintain when too many things are demanding attention at once. Sometimes the signal is still present, even when it becomes difficult to hear clearly.

name: Connection Refused
tech: Connection Refused is a specific TCP error. The rejection is clear, immediate, and definitive.
examples: A job application denied
An invitation declined
A breakup
Being cut off from further contact
A rejection from a romantic interest
reflection: Connection Refused is the case where a reachable system actively declines a request. Unlike silence or disconnection, the answer is clear. Human situations sometimes work the same way. A direct refusal can be disappointing, but it also removes uncertainty. Even painful clarity can be easier to live with than endless waiting.

name: Idle
tech: Idle is when a system has capacity available with nothing currently using it.
examples: A vacation
An evening with no obligations
A pause between projects
An open Saturday afternoon
Rest after hard work
reflection: Idle is when a system has available capacity but no immediate task to perform. The system is functional but at rest. Human life can feel similar during periods of inactivity. In cultures that equate usefulness with constant productivity, stillness can be mistaken for lack of purpose or value.

name: Throttled
tech: Throttling is when a system intentionally limits the rate of output.
situation: Holding back for practical or protective reasons.
examples: Hiding aspects of yourself while at work
Working at a slower speed to avoid overwhelming someone
Not sharing your creative ideas
Speaking carefully to avoid conflict
Editing yourself to avoid offending others
reflection: Throttling is when a system intentionally limits its own output. The system's full capacity is still present, but its output is being carefully regulated for practical reasons: preventing overload, conserving resources, or adapting to external limits. Human behavior often works the same way. People learn to hold back parts of themselves in certain environments or roles. Sometimes those self-imposed limitations remain in place long after they stop being necessary.

name: Buffer Full
tech: A buffer temporarily stores incoming data so a system can process it at a manageable rate. If more data arrives than the system can handle, the buffer eventually fills up.
examples: Drowning in unread messages
Falling behind on a growing todo list
Juggling too many commitments at once
Feeling unable to catch up
Jumping from one thing to the next without a break
reflection: A buffer temporarily holds incoming information until it can be processed. When too much information arrives too quickly, the buffer fills and the system begins struggling to keep up. Human life can feel similar during periods of sustained pressure or overload. Attention, energy, and emotional capacity all have limits.

name: Stale Cache
tech: A cache stores a copy of data so it can be retrieved quickly without going back to the original source.
situation: Going by what used to be true.
examples: Treating someone as the person they used to be
Returning to a place expecting it to be unchanged
Keeping an outdated self-image
Not seeing that a relationship has changed
Following social rules that have since evolved
Holding on to opinions you formed long ago
reflection: A cache stores previously retrieved information so it can be reused quickly. Problems appear when the stored version no longer matches the current reality. Human life can feel similar when old beliefs or expectations continue to affect how the present is perceived. Revising these outdated assumptions usually requires observing things as they currently are, as change is not always noticeable from the inside.

name: Memory Leak
tech: A memory leak is when a program holds onto memory past when it needs it.
examples: A recurring worry
A frequent regret
An unprocessed loss
Repeatedly reliving a painful experience
A nagging health issue
reflection: A memory leak happens when a system continues holding onto resources it no longer needs. The system keeps functioning, but over time this drain begins to affect performance. Human life can feel similar when unresolved worries, grief, or stress occupy more and more mental and emotional space. The result is often a growing sense of fatigue or heaviness that may be difficult to trace to any single cause.

name: Crash
tech: A crash is when a system stops running suddenly because of an error that broke it.
examples: A relationship that ended
A sudden loss in the family
An unexpected health crisis
A job or career ending abruptly
A mental or emotional breakdown
reflection: A crash is when a system stops suddenly before its current state can be fully preserved. Information that was never saved may be lost when the process ends abruptly. Human life can feel similar when something suddenly changes in a way that cannot be undone. Recovery is rarely as simple as restarting from where things left off. Life after a crash often means adapting to both what remains and what was lost.

name: Heartbeat
brief: A steady rhythm that keeps something alive.
tech: A heartbeat is a regular signal sent at fixed intervals so other systems know a process is still alive.
situation: A repeated action that sustains connection.
examples: Calling your parents every week
Going to therapy even when you feel fine
Following a daily routine
Walking the dog every morning
Tending to the basics of food, sleep, and movement
reflection: A heartbeat is a repeated signal that indicates a system is still functioning. The signal may seem small on its own, but over time its regularity becomes meaningful. Human life often works the same way. Relationships and routines are usually maintained through small, consistent actions.

name: Sync
tech: Sync is when two or more systems align in time so their actions happen together, or they reach the same state at once.
situation: Independent things aligning into coordinated action.
examples: A team working together effectively
A creative breakthrough from collaboration
Two people immediately understanding each other
An event coming together
Being on the same wavelength with someone else
reflection: Synchronization is the alignment of separate systems to work together effectively. Human situations sometimes work the same way. Good collaboration often depends on people, timing, and circumstances temporarily aligning.

name: Polling
tech: Polling is when a system repeatedly checks for a status update at regular intervals.
examples: Reloading your inbox waiting for a reply
Checking your phone repeatedly for a text
Watching for news of a pending event
Checking the mail for an expected package
Watching the door for someone to arrive
reflection: Polling is the repeated checking for updates at regular intervals, returning the same result unless something has changed. Human situations often work the same way during times of uncertainty or anticipation. Repeated checking may not change the outcome, but it can make waiting feel less passive.

name: Latency
brief: A long wait between action and result.
tech: Latency is the delay between when something is sent and when it arrives.
situation: Time passing between cause and effect.
examples: A message you sent that hasn't been answered yet
A decision whose consequences are still undetermined
A career move that hasn't paid off so far
A new habit that hasn't changed your life yet
A medical treatment that takes weeks to start working
reflection: Latency is the delay between an action and its observable result. Human life can feel similar at times when consequences or changes remain unknown. Uncertainty often encourages people to imagine possible outcomes, but an unresolved situation is not yet a final result.

name: Timeout
brief: Waiting for a response that never arrives.
tech: A timeout is when a system gives up waiting for a response. After a configured time, the request is treated as failed.
situation: Silence where an answer was expected.
examples: A job application that goes unanswered
A date request that gets ignored
A friendship that fades away
A promise that never gets fulfilled
An apology that never comes
reflection: A timeout occurs when a system stops waiting after no response arrives within a certain amount of time. The lack of a reply does not always indicate whether the message was ignored, missed, or never received. Human life can feel similar when silence leaves situations unresolved without an explanation. Sometimes the only decision available is whether to continue waiting.

name: Deadlock
brief: Both sides are stuck, each waiting for the other to make the first move.
tech: A deadlock is when two or more processes are each waiting for the other to release something.
situation: Two sides waiting for the other to take action.
examples: After an argument, friends waiting for each other to apologize
Two cars at an intersection, each waiting for the other to move first
A negotiation frozen with both sides waiting for the other to budge
Two people interested in each other, both waiting for the other to reach out
A meeting where no one wants to be the first to speak
reflection: A deadlock occurs when multiple systems are each waiting for the others before they can continue. As long as every side continues waiting, nothing changes. Human situations can work the same way when pride or caution prevent anyone from acting first. Deadlocks often persist until someone becomes willing to act without knowing how the other side will respond.

name: Patch
brief: A quick fix to keep things going for now.
tech: A patch is a small, quick change made to fix a specific problem.
examples: Patching a flat tire
Taking medicine for symptoms until you can determine the cause
Negotiating a temporary work arrangement
Apologizing to quickly end a conflict
Borrowing money to cover an unexpected expense
reflection: A patch is a small, localized change that fixes a specific problem without altering the underlying structure. The symptom goes away and the system runs again. Patches keep things going, but they accumulate, and a system covered in patches becomes harder to understand and harder to repair properly. Applying a patch can give you the time to design a proper fix.

name: Branch
tech: A branch is a divergent line of development that splits off from the main one.
examples: Keeping your current job or accepting a new offer
Committing to a relationship or remaining single
Speaking up about something or keeping it to yourself
Staying close to family or moving far away
Doing what you really want or what is expected of you
reflection: A branch is a divergent line of development that splits off from the main one. At a branching point, you can't fully know how each option will actually play out. You decide anyway, and the consequences follow over time.

name: Merge
brief: Two separate things are coming together.
tech: A merge is when two separate branches of work are combined into one.
examples: Reconnecting with a partner after time apart
Combining two separate work projects into one
Integrating your personal and professional lives
Moving in together
Two families becoming one
reflection: A merge is when two separate things become one. Becoming one changes both sides. The merged result is something that contains elements of both, but is also something new.

name: Garbage Collection
brief: Releasing what has served its purpose.
tech: Garbage collection is the automatic process by which a system reclaims memory that is no longer useful. The reclaimed space becomes available for new work.
situation: Time to clear out what is finished.
examples: Letting go of an old grudge
Giving away clothes you haven't worn in years
Quitting a habit you've outgrown
Releasing a friendship that's run its course
Donating books you've already read
reflection: Garbage collection is the process by which a system reclaims memory that nothing active still uses. Without periodic clearing, capacity stays committed to things that have already served their purpose. In computing, this clearing happens automatically. In life, the same work has to be done deliberately.

name: Upgrade
tech: An upgrade replaces a system with a newer version that has more capabilities or improvements.
situation: Replacing the old with something better.
examples: Getting better at something through practice
Moving into a home that better fits your needs
A new car that's more reliable
Stepping into a more challenging role
Personal growth from therapy
reflection: An upgrade replaces a system with a newer version that can do more. In computing, the upgrade is installed all at once. In life, it happens gradually, through what you experience and the work you put in.

name: Reset
tech: A reset returns a system to its starting state.
examples: Starting over after a major life change
Picking up the pieces after a relationship ends
Going back to school as an adult
Changing jobs or careers
Moving to a new home
reflection: A reset clears whatever has accumulated. Variables, configuration, working memory, all of it is wiped. In computing, the system returns to its original initial conditions. In life, a reset rarely returns you to exactly who you were before, as everything you've been through stays with you.
